verdict.alternative: O1 (plain unique index on email), only if a GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1 check returns zero rows, every write path already normalises email, and both incidents turn out to be exact-match races.

option_assessments.note: Do it. A unique index on lower(email) closes the check-then-insert race at the database, whatever code path inserts (V5). It also rejects case variants (V3), and it can serve the login lookup when the query uses the same expression (V3). Reconcile existing duplicates first. Build it with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction. Prefer the expression index to a citext column change, which needs a table-level ALTER.

It closes the exact-match race (V5), but Alice@x.com and alice@x.com still both get in, because a plain btree on text is case-sensitive. Only a lower() unique index blocks rows that differ only in case (V3). It is enough only if the data and every write path are already normalised.

On its own it cannot close the check-then-insert race. A test run showed two concurrent checks both seeing no row and both inserting, while a constraint allowed exactly one insert (V5). It also misses any write path that skips the logic. Idempotent upsert, unique-violation handling and account linking are worth doing alongside O2, not instead of it.
Two duplicate-account incidents this quarter (V2) show the current guards fail. Doing nothing leaves both the race and the case-variant gap open.

verdict.headline: Add a unique index on lower(email), built with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY after merging existing duplicates, and make the login query use the same lower(email) expression.
verdict.answer:
O2 is the right fix, and all three analysts reached it independently. A unique index on lower(email) enforces uniqueness in the database, which application logic cannot do. A test run reproduced the race: two concurrent checks both saw no row and both inserted, while a constraint allowed exactly one insert (V5). A lower() unique index also rejects addresses that differ only in case, which O1's plain index lets through, and it can serve logins when the query uses the same expression (V3).

Do these first, in order:
1. Measure. Run GROUP BY email and GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1, and check pg_indexes to see which indexes users already has.
2. Pull the rows from the two incidents and classify each: exact duplicate (a race), a case or whitespace variant, or two different emails.
3. Deploy write-time normalisation (lower and trim in one shared function), plus handling for SQLSTATE 23505 (unique violation) on signup, OAuth callback and email change.
4. Merge the existing duplicates. Treat this as a product and security decision: auto-merge only where both sides are verified.
5. Re-run the duplicate check, then run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ... ON users (lower(email)) outside any transaction.
6. Confirm pg_index.indisvalid is true. Run EXPLAIN on the login SQL the ORM actually generates before dropping the old plain email index.

The incident classification is the fact that changes the scope. If either incident involved two different emails (OAuth relay addresses, a work and a personal address, or an email change), O2 is still worth shipping but will not stop that kind of duplicate. That needs separate account linking keyed on verified email or the provider's user ID. Auth0 documents that the same person signing up through different providers becomes separate users by default (V4). If rows are soft-deleted or scoped by tenant, make the index partial (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or composite (tenant_id, lower(email)), and give the login query the same predicate.
why: A test run confirmed that application-only check-then-insert is racy: two concurrent checks both saw no row and both inserted. A unique constraint allowed exactly one insert, so enforcement belongs in the database (V5).

The PostgreSQL docs confirm that a unique index on lower(col) rejects rows that differ only in case, and that the planner uses it when the query matches the same expression. So O2 prevents more duplicates than O1 and still serves logins (V3).
All three analysts chose O2 independently, and the red team found it holds up with changes. No verification record contradicts a load-bearing claim behind it.

The PostgreSQL docs, fetched by all three analysts, say CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not block writes during the build. It must run outside a transaction, and it leaves an INVALID index behind if duplicates remain. That makes the migration safe at 4M rows once the data is reconciled.

caveats.text: Merge or rename existing exact and case/whitespace duplicates, and re-check immediately before the build. Otherwise the unique build fails and leaves an INVALID index that still enforces uniqueness and slows writes.

Run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction block. Most migration tools wrap migrations in one by default, so turn that off (Rails disable_ddl_transaction!, Django atomic=False). Set a statement timeout and watch for idle-in-transaction sessions, because the build waits for them.

Make the login query and every write path use the same expression as the index, lower(email) = lower($1). Otherwise the index is not used and logins may fall back to a sequential scan. Django iexact generates UPPER(), which will not use a lower() index. Run EXPLAIN on the real generated SQL before dropping the old index.

Classify the two incidents. If either involved different email addresses (OAuth or relay addresses, email changes), O2 will not prevent that kind of duplicate. Add account linking keyed on verified email or the provider's user ID.
Handle SQLSTATE 23505 (unique violation) at signup, OAuth callback and email change. Show 'account exists' or a link flow, not a 500. Ship this before the index goes in.

If rows are soft-deleted, scoped by tenant, or can have a null email, use a partial index (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or a composite one (tenant_id, lower(email)), and give the login query the same predicate.

red_team_responses.detail: Classifying the incident rows is now a do-alongside step. O2 ships either way, because it closes the race (V5) and case variants (V3). If either incident involved two different emails, account linking keyed on verified email or the provider's user ID becomes a separate workstream (V4).

Use one normalise() function in shared code for both writes and the login lookup. Match the index expression to the SQL the ORM actually emits (V3). Run EXPLAIN on the login query before dropping the old index, and alert on sequential scans of users.

Order the rollout: normalisation and 23505 handling first, then reconcile duplicates, then re-check, then the concurrent build outside a transaction with timeouts, then check indisvalid (drop concurrently and retry if false). Prefer the expression index. If a normalised column is wanted, add a plain column and backfill it in batches rather than adding a stored generated column, which rewrites the table.

Treat the merge as a product and security decision. Auto-merge only pairs where both sides are verified, move child rows inside a transaction, keep an audit table, and send the rest to manual review. Never auto-link OAuth to an unverified local account, and expire unverified signups.

Settle uniqueness scope from the table's DDL before building. Use a partial (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or composite (tenant_id, lower(email)) unique index as the data model requires, with a matching login predicate.

where_council_may_be_wrong: The two incidents may not involve email equality at all (OAuth relay addresses, different addresses, email changes). Then O2 is good hygiene but does not fix the bugs that actually happened.
Email may not be a one-per-account identity key (shared B2B inboxes, phone-only accounts, several emails per user). A global unique index on email would then be the wrong shape.
The legacy duplicates may be too many or too tangled to merge soon, which delays the full index.
verdict.what_council_may_be_missing: No analyst saw the actual schema, data, login query, ORM or incident reports. So it is unconfirmed whether email is nullable, soft-deleted or tenant-scoped, whether an index already exists, how many duplicates exist, and what caused the two bugs. The recommendation rests on general PostgreSQL behaviour, not on this system.
verdict.cost_if_council_wrong: If the incidents came from identity-provider or different-address signups, the team spends a merge and migration effort and still gets a third duplicate-account bug. If the rollout is careless, the costs are login latency regressions, users locked out by case-sensitive matching, 500 errors on signup, or data lost or accounts exposed through careless merging.
what_would_change_verdict: The incident rows show different email addresses for the same person, not addresses equal under lower(trim(email)). Account linking then becomes the primary fix, with O2 as a secondary backstop.
GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1 returns zero rows, every write path already normalises email, and both incidents were exact-match races. O1 would then be simpler and just as good.
The users DDL or product rules show email is not a one-per-account key (shared inboxes, several emails per user). A global unique index would then be the wrong design.
verdict.confidence_basis: The mechanisms are verified: the race was reproduced (V5), and the docs confirm the expression index behaviour (V3) and the concurrent-build behaviour. All three analysts agreed independently. But the root cause of the two incidents, the current duplicate counts and the uniqueness scope are unknown, and any of these could shrink O2 from "the fix" to "a necessary backstop". The confidence ceiling is medium.
verdict.recommended: O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the email (e.g. lower(email) expression index or citext column), after reconciling existing duplicates

failure_modes.scenario: The index shipped, but the two incidents were never checked. They turn out to be OAuth/SSO versus password signups under different addresses (for example an Apple 'Hide My Email' relay, or a work and a personal address), Gmail dot or plus aliases, or an email-change flow. lower(trim(email)) treats those as different, so a third duplicate-account bug arrives in month four. The index worked as designed; it just did not fix what caused these bugs. The council's own earlier intake (council-workspace/iteration-1/eval-2-user-is-actually-right/with_skill/outputs/report.md) raised this exact question and never answered it. Auth0's docs (V4) confirm that multi-provider signup creates separate users by default.
failure_modes.factual_claim: In both incidents this quarter, the duplicate users rows have emails that are equal under lower(trim(email)). Check by pulling the incident rows and comparing lower(trim(email)) across each pair.
failure_modes.mitigation: Before calling O2 'the fix', pull the incident rows and classify each one: an exact duplicate (race), a case or whitespace variant, or a different email. Ship O2 either way, because it closes the race and the case variants. If either incident involved different emails, open a separate workstream for identity linking keyed on verified email or provider subject.

failure_modes.scenario: The lookup and the index drift apart. Writes are normalised, but the login query stays 'WHERE email = $1' or uses Django's email__iexact. On PostgreSQL, Django compiles iexact to UPPER(email::text) = UPPER(%s), which cannot use a lower(email) index. One of two things follows. If someone drops the old plain email index as 'redundant', every login sequentially scans 4M rows and p99 login latency collapses. If the old index stays, login becomes effectively case-sensitive against lowercased stored values, and users who type 'Alice@x.com' get 'user not found'.
failure_modes.factual_claim: django/db/backends/postgresql/base.py maps 'iexact' to '= UPPER(%s)'. The PostgreSQL docs (indexes-expressional.html, V3) say an expression index is used only when the query predicate matches the indexed expression.
failure_modes.mitigation: Put one normalise() function in shared code and use it in both the write paths and the login lookup. Make the index expression match the expression the ORM actually emits: Upper() if the app uses Django iexact, Lower() if the query calls lower() explicitly. Run EXPLAIN on the exact generated login SQL before dropping any existing index, and alert on seq scans of users.

failure_modes.scenario: The rollout goes wrong. Duplicates are cleaned up, but the still-unfixed signup path inserts new ones before the build runs. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY then fails and leaves an INVALID index. The planner ignores that index, yet it still costs update overhead and keeps enforcing uniqueness. Signup, OAuth callback and email-change paths start throwing unhandled 23505 errors, which show up as 500s, before anyone believes the constraint exists. Separately, the migration framework wraps the DDL in a transaction and it errors out, or the build hangs waiting on an idle-in-transaction session. If the team picks the 'normalised column' variant as ADD COLUMN ... GENERATED ALWAYS AS (lower(email)) STORED, PostgreSQL rewrites the whole 4M-row table and its indexes under lock.
failure_modes.factual_claim: The PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX docs say a failed concurrent unique build leaves an 'invalid' index that 'continues to enforce its uniqueness constraint afterwards'. They also say uniqueness is enforced against other transactions from the second scan onward, that CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block, and that the build waits for all existing transactions. The ALTER TABLE docs (PG 18) say adding a stored generated column rewrites the entire table and its indexes.
failure_modes.mitigation: Work in this order. (1) Deploy write-time normalisation plus handling of 23505 (unique-violation), mapped to 'email already registered' or a link flow, on every write path. (2) Reconcile existing duplicates. (3) Re-run the GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1 check immediately before the build. (4) Run the build outside a transaction (Django AddIndexConcurrently with atomic=False, Rails disable_ddl_transaction!), with a statement timeout and with idle-in-transaction sessions killed. (5) Confirm pg_index.indisvalid afterwards, and on failure drop the index concurrently and retry. For a normalised column, backfill a plain column in batches instead of adding a stored generated column.

failure_modes.scenario: Reconciliation or the new uniqueness rule causes a security or data-loss incident. An automated merge keeps the wrong survivor, orphans orders or subscriptions, or merges an attacker's unverified pre-registered account into the victim's verified one. That is the 'classic-federated merge' pre-account-hijacking pattern. Once email is unique, an unverified squatter registration also blocks the real owner. If the OAuth callback does 'find user by email and log in', it hands the victim's SSO session to the attacker's pre-created account.
failure_modes.factual_claim: The users table (or the auth flow) separates verified from unverified emails, and the OAuth callback currently links to an existing user by email match alone. Check the schema and the callback code. The attack class is documented in Sudhodanan and Paverd, 'Pre-hijacked Accounts', USENIX Security 2022.
failure_modes.mitigation: Treat the merge as a product and security decision, as Analyst 2 said. Auto-merge only pairs where both sides are verified, pick the survivor deterministically, move child rows inside a transaction and keep an audit table. Send everything else to manual review. Never auto-link OAuth to an unverified local account. Expire unverified signups so squatting cannot hold an address.

failure_modes.scenario: The uniqueness scope is wrong for the data model. The table soft-deletes rows (deleted_at) or is multi-tenant. A global unique index on lower(email) then blocks legitimate re-signup after account deletion, or blocks the same person from belonging to two tenants. Support tickets pile up and someone drops the index under pressure. A partial index added as a fix (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) serves the login query only if the query carries the same predicate.
failure_modes.factual_claim: The users table has a soft-delete column, or an organisation/tenant column that scopes identity. Check the users table's DDL.
failure_modes.mitigation: Settle the scope before building. Use UNIQUE (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, or UNIQUE (tenant_id, lower(email)), as the model requires, and give the login query the same predicate. If the citext variant is chosen, note that its docs recommend nondeterministic collations instead and that its case-folding depends on the database's LC_CTYPE.

red_team.conditions_where_leader_right:
The recommendation is right when all of the following hold:
- The system is PostgreSQL (V1) and users log in with one email per account, across the whole system or within a tenant.
- The duplicates come at least partly from the check-then-insert race (V5) or from case and whitespace variants of the same address.
- Existing duplicates can be reconciled, and the survivor rules for accounts that own data are agreed.
- Every write path and the login lookup can use the same normalisation expression that the index uses.
- The migration can run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction, after unique-violation (23505) handling has shipped.

Under those conditions the index is the only fix that holds in the database whatever code path inserts. It is also cheap on 4M rows and can double as the login index. None of the failure modes found is a reason not to do it.
red_team.conditions_where_leader_wrong:
The recommendation is wrong, or at best incomplete, when:
- The incidents came from different email addresses: OAuth relay or private addresses, a work address versus a personal one, or email changes. There O2 is necessary but does not fix those bugs, and presenting it as the fix is the error. The fix is identity linking keyed on verified email or provider subject.
- Email is not the identity key: users can have several emails, accounts can lack an email (phone-only), or several accounts legitimately share an address, as with shared team inboxes in B2B.
- Uniqueness must be scoped, by tenant or to rows that are not soft-deleted. A global index is then the wrong shape; a composite or partial one is needed.
- The legacy duplicates are too many or too tangled to reconcile soon. A full unique index cannot be built then; an interim partial index over new rows only is weaker and does not catch a new row that duplicates an old one.
- The ORM's lookup cannot be made to match the index expression, and the team cannot keep a second index for it.

ballots.answer:
My pick is O2: a unique index on lower(email) (or on a normalised column), built with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY once existing duplicates have been merged. It fixes the problem in the database itself, which O3 cannot. Application locks and upserts still let races and forgotten signup paths through. O4 changes nothing. O1 does stop the exact-match race, but Alice@x.com and alice@x.com would still both get in. That case-and-whitespace mismatch is a very common cause of duplicate accounts.

Rollout:
1. Find the duplicates now. Run GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1, and merge or rename those accounts. This is a product decision because the merged accounts own data.
2. Make every write path normalise the email (trim and lowercase), and backfill the column.
3. Run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY users_email_lower_uq ON users (lower(email)). Run it outside any transaction, so turn off your migration tool's transaction wrapper. At 4M rows this is a minutes-scale build that doesn't block writes.
4. If the build fails, it leaves an INVALID index behind that still enforces uniqueness. Check pg_index.indisvalid, drop the index, fix the rows, and retry.
5. Change the login query to WHERE lower(email)=lower($1) so it uses the new index. Then drop the old plain index on email if nothing else uses it.
6. Catch unique-violation errors (SQLSTATE 23505) at signup and on email change,

conditions.text: Before building the index, find and merge or rename existing duplicates, both exact and case/whitespace-insensitive. Otherwise the build fails and leaves an INVALID index behind.
Run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction block. Most migration tools wrap migrations in a transaction by default, so disable that for this migration.
Change the login query and all writes to use the same normalised expression, lower(email) or a normalised column. Otherwise the planner won't use the index and lookups get slower.
Handle SQLSTATE 23505 unique violations at signup and on email change so users see a proper message instead of a 500 error.
If email is nullable, or soft-deleted or multi-tenant rows can legitimately share an email, use a partial index (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or a composite one (tenant_id, lower(email)).
Find the root cause of the two bugs from the incident reports. If it was OAuth or identity-provider mismatch, or email changes, add account linking by provider subject ID.

ballots.answer: O2, likely favored by whoever proposed "add a unique index" but got the normalization detail right. A DB-level uniqueness constraint is the correct root fix: it's atomic under concurrent inserts, which app-only logic (O3) is not -- that race is a classic source of duplicate-account bugs. But O1 (exact-match) often misses the actual duplicates: "same person" duplicates are usually case/whitespace variants (Foo@x.com vs foo@x.com), not byte-identical strings, so an exact unique index gives false confidence. Use a unique index on lower(trim(email)) (or citext) after reconciling existing dupes, built with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (no write lock, but fails/invalid if dupes remain -- verified against PG docs). Point the login query at the same normalized expression so it stays index-backed. Keep app-level idempotent upsert/graceful unique_violation handling too -- defense in depth, not a replacement.

report_markdown:
**Council verdict: Partly.** Add a unique index on lower(email), built with CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY after merging existing duplicates, and make the login query use the same lower(email) expression.
Confidence: **medium**. The mechanisms are verified: the race was reproduced (V5), and the docs confirm the expression index behaviour (V3) and the concurrent-build behaviour. All three analysts agreed independently. But the root cause of the two incidents, the current duplicate counts and the uniqueness scope are unknown, and any of these could shrink O2 from "the fix" to "a necessary backstop". The confidence ceiling is medium.

**What you asked:** Whether adding a unique index (constraint) on the users.email column in the ~4M-row Postgres users table is the right way to prevent the same person from ending up with duplicate accounts, given that email is looked up on every login and two duplicate-account incidents occurred this quarter. → **what you're after:** Prevent duplicate accounts per person at the data layer, with a safe rollout on a live, heavily-queried table.
_Reading check:_ R1/R3/R4 aren't really separable here: the four options already encode "is a unique index right" (R1/R2), "is it sufficient alone" (R4), and "how to build it safely" (R3) as a single choice. I answere

**Recommendation:** O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the email (e.g. lower(email) expression index or citext column), after reconciling existing duplicates

### Answer
O2 is the right fix, and all three analysts reached it independently. A unique index on lower(email) enforces uniqueness in the database, which application logic cannot do. A test run reproduced the race: two concurrent checks both saw no row and both inserted, while a constraint allowed exactly one insert (V5). A lower() unique index also rejects addresses that differ only in case, which O1's plain index lets through, and it can serve logins when the query uses the same expression (V3).

Do these first, in order:
1. Measure. Run GROUP BY email and GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1, and check pg_indexes to see which indexes users already has.
2. Pull the rows from the two incidents and classify each: exact duplicate (a race), a case or whitespace variant, or two different emails.
3. Deploy write-time normalisation (lower and trim in one shared function), plus handling for SQLSTATE 23505 (unique violation) on signup, OAuth callback and email change.
4. Merge the existing duplicates. Treat this as a product and security decision: auto-merge only where both sides are verified.
5. Re-run the duplicate check, then run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ... ON users (lower(email)) outside any transaction.
6. Confirm pg_index.indisvalid is true. Run EXPLAIN on the login SQL the ORM actually generates before dropping the old plain email index.

The incident classification is the fact that changes the scope. If either incident involved two different emails (OAuth relay addresses, a work and a personal address, or an email change), O2 is still worth shipping but will not stop that kind of duplicate. That needs separate account linking keyed on verified email or the provider's user ID. Auth0 documents that the same person signing up through different providers becomes separate users by default (V4). If rows are soft-deleted or scoped by tenant, make the index partial (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or composite (tenant_id, lower(email)), and give the login query the same predicate.

### Why
- A test run confirmed that application-only check-then-insert is racy: two concurrent checks both saw no row and both inserted. A unique constraint allowed exactly one insert, so enforcement belongs in the database (V5).
- The PostgreSQL docs confirm that a unique index on lower(col) rejects rows that differ only in case, and that the planner uses it when the query matches the same expression. So O2 prevents more duplicates than O1 and still serves logins (V3).
- All three analysts chose O2 independently, and the red team found it holds up with changes. No verification record contradicts a load-bearing claim behind it.
- The PostgreSQL docs, fetched by all three analysts, say CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not block writes during the build. It must run outside a transaction, and it leaves an INVALID index behind if duplicates remain. That makes the migration safe at 4M rows once the data is reconciled.

### Do these first
- **blocking** (seat consensus): Merge or rename existing exact and case/whitespace duplicates, and re-check immediately before the build. Otherwise the unique build fails and leaves an INVALID index that still enforces uniqueness and slows writes.
- **blocking** (seat consensus): Run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction block. Most migration tools wrap migrations in one by default, so turn that off (Rails disable_ddl_transaction!, Django atomic=False). Set a statement timeout and watch for idle-in-transaction sessions, because the build waits for them.
- **do alongside** (verified, V3): Make the login query and every write path use the same expression as the index, lower(email) = lower($1). Otherwise the index is not used and logins may fall back to a sequential scan. Django iexact generates UPPER(), which will not use a lower() index. Run EXPLAIN on the real generated SQL before dropping the old index.
- **do alongside** (verified, V4): Classify the two incidents. If either involved different email addresses (OAuth or relay addresses, email changes), O2 will not prevent that kind of duplicate. Add account linking keyed on verified email or the provider's user ID.
- **do alongside** (seat consensus): Handle SQLSTATE 23505 (unique violation) at signup, OAuth callback and email change. Show 'account exists' or a link flow, not a 500. Ship this before the index goes in.
- **do alongside** (seat consensus): If rows are soft-deleted, scoped by tenant, or can have a null email, use a partial index (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) or a composite one (tenant_id, lower(email)), and give the login query the same predicate.

### Where you and the council disagree
You said: "I want to add a unique index on users.email. Good idea?"
Council recommends: O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the email (e.g. lower(email) expression index or citext column), after reconciling existing duplicates
Why: A test run confirmed that application-only check-then-insert is racy: two concurrent checks both saw no row and both inserted. A unique constraint allowed exactly one insert, so enforcement belongs in the database (V5). The PostgreSQL docs confirm that a unique index on lower(col) rejects rows that differ only in case, and that the planner uses it when the query matches the same expression. So O2 prevents more duplicates than O1 and still serves logins (V3). All three analysts chose O2 independently, and the red team found it holds up with changes. No verification record contradicts a load-bearing claim behind it. The PostgreSQL docs, fetched by all three analysts, say CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY does not block writes during the build. It must run outside a transaction, and it leaves an INVALID index behind if duplicates remain. That makes the migration safe at 4M rows once the data is reconciled.
What the council may be missing: No analyst saw the actual schema, data, login query, ORM or incident reports. So it is unconfirmed whether email is nullable, soft-deleted or tenant-scoped, whether an index already exists, how many duplicates exist, and what caused the two bugs. The recommendation rests on general PostgreSQL behaviour, not on this system.
Cost if the council is wrong: If the incidents came from identity-provider or different-address signups, the team spends a merge and migration effort and still gets a third duplicate-account bug. If the rollout is careless, the costs are login latency regressions, users locked out by case-sensitive matching, 500 errors on signup, or data lost or accounts exposed through careless merging.
Your call stays the default until you decide otherwise.

### Minority report
None: the analysts reached the same answer independently (all Claude models, so treat it as one model family's view).

### Where the council may be wrong
- The two incidents may not involve email equality at all (OAuth relay addresses, different addresses, email changes). Then O2 is good hygiene but does not fix the bugs that actually happened.
- Email may not be a one-per-account identity key (shared B2B inboxes, phone-only accounts, several emails per user). A global unique index on email would then be the wrong shape.
- The legacy duplicates may be too many or too tangled to merge soon, which delays the full index.

### What would change this verdict
- The incident rows show different email addresses for the same person, not addresses equal under lower(trim(email)). Account linking then becomes the primary fix, with O2 as a secondary backstop.
- GROUP BY lower(trim(email)) HAVING count(*)>1 returns zero rows, every write path already normalises email, and both incidents were exact-match races. O1 would then be simpler and just as good.
- The users DDL or product rules show email is not a one-per-account key (shared inboxes, several emails per user). A global unique index would then be the wrong design.

#### How the council ran
- Mode: standard. Seats: first_principles (Claude fable): O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the email (e., high; premise_auditor (Claude opus): O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the email (e., high; practitioner (Claude sonnet): O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the email (e., medium.
- Blind vote: O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the 3. Final: O2: Add a unique index on a normalised form of the 3.
- Claims verified with tools: 5 (4 true, 1 partly).
- Escalations run: premise_audit, verify, red_team, audit.
- Red team (Claude opus): withstands_with_changes.
- Diversity: All voting seats were Claude models, so their agreement is one model family's view. Audit: passed.
- Agents: 15.
- Claude's own view before the council (never shown to the council): Yes: add it, but case-insensitively (lower(email) or citext), dedupe existing rows first, build CONCURRENTLY, and handle the unique violation in the app.
